denomProfiles/brethren-in-christ/tagline: Anabaptist, Pietist and Wesleyan streams joined in one evangelical peace church.
denomProfiles/brethren-in-christ/coreDoc: Personal conversion and new birth, from its Pietist roots.
Wesleyan-holiness teaching of sanctification, adopted in the early twentieth century.
Nonresistance and peacemaking from Anabaptist tradition.
Obedient discipleship within a caring church community.
denomProfiles/brethren-in-christ/focuses: Evangelism and church planting, especially in southern Africa and South Asia.
Higher education through Messiah University (founded 1909, Grantham, Pennsylvania).
Holding together Anabaptist, Pietist and Wesleyan emphases.
denomProfiles/brethren-in-christ/practic: Foot washing observed with the Lord's Supper.
General Conference with bishops (regional overseers) and local congregations.
Contemporary evangelical worship in many North American churches.
Membership in the Mennonite World Conference.
denomProfiles/brethren-in-christ/influen: Brethren in Christ in Zimbabwe and Zambia
Missions from 1898 grew into churches now larger than the North American body.
Conservative groups that separated in the nineteenth century to keep older ways.
denomProfiles/brethren-in-christ/keyFigu: Early leader of the River Brethren in the 1770s-1780s
Pioneer missionary to Matopo, Southern Rhodesia (1898)
denomProfiles/brethren-in-christ/inIndia: Brethren in Christ missionaries began work in Bihar in 1914, around Saharsa and Madhepura; the Indian church has since spread into Odisha and other states.
denomProfiles/baptist/tagline: Believer's baptism, gathered congregations and religious liberty for all.
denomProfiles/baptist/coreDoctrines/0: The Bible as the final authority for faith and practice.
denomProfiles/baptist/coreDoctrines/1: Baptism by immersion only for those who profess faith.
denomProfiles/baptist/coreDoctrines/2: A regenerate church membership gathered in local, self-governing congregations.
denomProfiles/baptist/coreDoctrines/3: The priesthood of all believers and soul liberty.
denomProfiles/baptist/coreDoctrines/4: Religious freedom and the separation of church and state.
denomProfiles/baptist/coreDoctrines/5: Two ordinances, baptism and the Lord's Supper, understood as obedience and witness.
denomProfiles/baptist/focuses/0: Evangelism and world mission, from William Carey's Baptist Missionary Society (1792) onwards.
denomProfiles/baptist/focuses/1: Preaching as the centre of worship.
denomProfiles/baptist/focuses/2: Freedom of conscience and opposition to established churches.
denomProfiles/baptist/focuses/3: Voluntary association of churches in unions and conventions.
denomProfiles/baptist/practices/0: Immersion of believers, often in a baptistry in the church.
denomProfiles/baptist/practices/1: Lord's Supper monthly or quarterly, as a memorial.
denomProfiles/baptist/practices/2: Church meetings in which members vote on pastors and business.
denomProfiles/baptist/practices/3: Confessions (e.g. 1644, 1677/1689, the Baptist Faith and Message) used as guides, not creeds.
denomProfiles/baptist/practices/4: Associations and the Baptist World Alliance (1905) linking churches.
denomProfiles/baptist/influenced/0/text: Baptists became one of the largest evangelical families.
denomProfiles/baptist/influenced/1/text: The Campbells worked within Baptist associations between 1815 and 1830.
denomProfiles/baptist/influenced/2/text: Many early Adventists, including William Miller, were Baptists.
denomProfiles/baptist/influenced/3/text: Baptist campaigners such as John Leland and Isaac Backus pressed for religious liberty.
denomProfiles/baptist/keyFigures/0/role: Founded the first Baptist church, Amsterdam 1609
denomProfiles/baptist/keyFigures/1/role: Brought the first Baptist church to England (1612) and pleaded for liberty of conscience
denomProfiles/baptist/keyFigures/2/role: Founded Providence and the first Baptist church in America (1638-39)
denomProfiles/baptist/keyFigures/3/role: Pioneer of modern Protestant missions in India
denomProfiles/baptist/members/note: Approximate baptised membership of churches in the Baptist World Alliance's member bodies, as published by the BWA; the wider Baptist community, including children and non-BWA bodies, is larger.
denomProfiles/baptist/inIndia: Baptist churches are largest in North-East India: most Christians in Nagaland and many in Manipur, Meghalaya (Garo Hills) and southern Mizoram are Baptist, alongside older Telugu Baptist churches in Andhra Pradesh from the American Baptist mission and the Serampore legacy in Bengal.
denomProfiles/general-baptists/tagline: The first English Baptists, teaching that Christ died for all.
denomProfiles/general-baptists/coreDoctr: General atonement: Christ died for all people, not only the elect.
Liberty of conscience for all, including non-Christians (Helwys, 1612).
The Standard Confession (1660) and the Orthodox Creed (1679).
Laying on of hands for the newly baptised, taught as a principle in Hebrews 6 by many congregations.
denomProfiles/general-baptists/focuses/2: Evangelical revival in the New Connexion (1770) under Dan Taylor.
denomProfiles/general-baptists/focuses/3: Mission in Orissa through the General Baptist Missionary Society (1816).
denomProfiles/general-baptists/practices: Messengers serving several churches, and a General Assembly from the 1650s.
Plain worship; many early congregations opposed congregational hymn singing.
Church discipline exercised by the members.
denomProfiles/general-baptists/influence: Many Old Connexion churches drifted into Unitarianism in the eighteenth century.
American Arminian Baptists continue the General Baptist line.
The New Connexion united with Particular Baptists in 1891.
denomProfiles/general-baptists/keyFigure: Se-baptised and founded the first Baptist church (1609)
Author of A Short Declaration of the Mistery of Iniquity (1612)
Leading seventeenth-century General Baptist writer and messenger
Founder of the evangelical New Connexion (1770)
denomProfiles/general-baptists/inIndia: The New Connexion's General Baptist Missionary Society sent missionaries to Cuttack, Orissa (Odisha), from 1822; the churches it founded later joined the Church of North India (1970).
denomProfiles/particular-baptists/taglin: Calvinistic Baptists of the London Confessions and the modern missionary movement.
denomProfiles/particular-baptists/coreDo: Particular (definite) redemption: Christ died effectually for the elect.
Reformed teaching on grace and the sovereignty of God.
Believer's baptism by immersion, practised from about 1641.
The First (1644) and Second (1677, reissued 1689) London Confessions.
Covenant theology adapted to a gathered church of believers.
denomProfiles/particular-baptists/focuse: World mission, after Andrew Fuller rebutted hyper-Calvinism.
Liberty of conscience under the Restoration and after.
Debate between strict and open communion.
denomProfiles/particular-baptists/practi: Congregational government with elders and deacons.
Hymn singing, defended by Benjamin Keach against much opposition in the 1690s.
Associations of churches meeting regularly for counsel.
denomProfiles/particular-baptists/influe: Founded at Kettering in 1792, sending William Carey to India.
Its 1742 Philadelphia Confession carried the London Confession to America.
Modern Calvinistic Baptists continue the 1689 Confession.
Early Southern Baptists drew on this Calvinist heritage.
denomProfiles/particular-baptists/keyFig: London merchant and pastor, signatory of the 1644 Confession
Pastor and catechist who championed hymn singing
Author of The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785)
Victorian preacher at the Metropolitan Tabernacle
denomProfiles/particular-baptists/inIndi: William Carey reached Bengal in 1793; the Serampore mission (from 1800) of Carey, Marshman and Ward translated the Bible into many Indian languages and founded Serampore College (1818). BMS-related churches in Bengal and Odisha largely joined the Church of North India in 1970.
denomProfiles/southern-baptist-conventio: America's largest Protestant denomination, built on missions and cooperative giving.
The Baptist Faith and Message (1925, revised 1963 and 2000) as its confession.
Biblical inerrancy, affirmed in the 2000 revision.
Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ.
Local church autonomy and believer's baptism by immersion.
Complementarian teaching: the office of pastor is limited to men (2000).
Evangelism and church planting through the North American Mission Board.
Foreign missions through the International Mission Board.
Funding through the Cooperative Program (1925).
Theological education in six seminaries.
Public engagement on religious liberty and moral issues via the Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission.
Annual meeting of messengers sent by cooperating churches.
Revival-style invitations and altar calls in many churches.
Sunday School and Vacation Bible School.
Lottie Moon Christmas Offering for international missions.
Lord's Supper as a memorial, usually quarterly or monthly.
Cooperative Baptist Fellowship
Moderates formed the CBF (1991) after the conservative resurgence.
Baptist missions worldwide
Its missionaries planted many national conventions, including in Nigeria and Brazil.
Brazilian Baptist Convention
Grew from Southern Baptist missionaries in Brazil from 1881.
William Bullein Johnson
First president (1845)
Lottie Moon
Missionary to China, namesake of the mission offering
E. Y. Mullins
Theologian and seminary president; framed soul competency
Adrian Rogers
Pastor whose 1979 election began the conservative resurgence
Billy Graham
Southern Baptist evangelist
Reported membership in the 2024 Annual Church Profile compiled by Lifeway Research; weekly attendance is far lower.
Southern Baptist missionaries have worked in India mainly through medical and church-planting ministries; Bangalore Baptist Hospital, opened in 1973, is the best-known institution.
denomProfiles/national-baptist-conventio: The largest African American denomination: church, school and civil-rights base.
Evangelical Baptist faith: salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as ordinances.
Autonomy of the local church within a voluntary national convention.
Scripture as the rule of faith, broadly following the New Hampshire Confession (1833).
Black self-help, education and economic uplift.
Foreign missions in Africa and the Caribbean.
Publishing through its own Sunday School Publishing Board.
Civil rights and social justice, debated sharply in the 1950s-1960s.
Expressive preaching, gospel music and call-and-response worship.
Annual session of messengers and a strong presidency.
Women's missionary and educational work (Woman's Convention, 1900).
Communion monthly in many churches, often on the first Sunday.
National Baptist Convention of America
Separated in 1915 after a dispute over the publishing house.
Progressive National Baptist Convention
Formed in 1961 by Baptists, including King, who backed direct civil-rights action.
Civil-rights movement
Many leaders of the movement were National Baptist pastors.
Elias Camp Morris
First president (1895-1922)
Nannie Helen Burroughs
Leader of the Woman's Convention and educator
Joseph H. Jackson
President 1953-1982, who opposed civil-disobedience tactics
Martin Luther King Jr.
Raised in a National Baptist church; later Progressive
denomProfiles/american-baptist-churches-: Mainline, multi-ethnic Baptists rooted in the first national mission societies.
Believer's baptism and the Lord's Supper as ordinances.
Soul liberty and freedom of conscience; no binding creed.
Scripture as the authoritative guide, interpreted in community.
Local church autonomy within regional and national bodies.
Home and foreign missions, from the Triennial Convention (1814).
Racial and ethnic diversity in its congregations.
Ecumenism: a member of the National Council of Churches and the World Council of Churches.
Social justice, from Walter Rauschenbusch's Social Gospel onward.
Regions and a Biennial Mission Summit linking autonomous churches.
Ordination of women as pastors.
Varied worship, from traditional to contemporary and ethnic-language congregations.
Lord's Supper commonly monthly.
Baptist missions in Asia
Missions to Burma (Judson, 1813), North-East India and Andhra planted large Baptist churches.
Conservative Baptist Association
Formed (1947) by conservatives who left during fundamentalist-modernist disputes.
General Association of Regular Baptist Churches
Fundamentalist Baptists who withdrew in 1932.
Adoniram and Ann Hasseltine Judson
Missionaries to Burma whose call prompted the Triennial Convention
Luther Rice
Organiser of national Baptist support for missions
Walter Rauschenbusch
Social Gospel theologian
Harry Emerson Fosdick
Liberal preacher of Riverside Church

American Baptist missionaries reached Assam in 1836 and the Naga Hills from 1872, and began the Telugu mission at Nellore (1840), where thousands were baptised at Ongole in 1878; the Council of Baptist Churches in North East India and Telugu Baptist bodies grew from this work.
